title: Can prefetch make xswap reads faster?
subtitle: Two ways to read pages before demand — their motivation, implementation and measured cost

verdict.headline: Neither candidate is ready to advance

sections.title: The problem: each missing page can stop the application
sections.lead: When a needed page is outside RAM, the application faults and waits for it to return. Xswap gives that page a virtual swap slot: its contents may be compressed in RAM or written back to disk.

blocks.takeaway: Original path in this 4 KiB test: fetch on demand

blocks.text: The baseline routes xswap through synchronous demand reads and skips ordinary readahead. That is reasonable for cheap in-memory reads, but written-back pages now require disk I/O. Sequential access may expose avoidable waiting.

blocks.takeaway: Two different costs motivated two independent changes
rows: Upcoming sequential accesses are predictable. Fetching neighbors could hide disk waiting.
Check physical backing; route those faults through existing readahead. Speculative xswap neighbors must also have physical backing.
Neighbors could enter the swap cache early, potentially reducing repeated demand-fault overhead.
Check actual zswap residency; prefetch compressed neighbors into the swap cache. Each page is still decompressed synchronously.

blocks.takeaway: Changed path: one fault also prepares likely next pages

blocks.text: Both patches start from the same descriptor-lifetime repair; they are not stacked. The goal is lower application read latency. The tradeoff is extra work on the current fault, especially when neighbors are not needed.

sections.title: 1. Read disk-backed pages ahead
sections.lead: Idea: fetch nearby disk pages before they are needed. Sequential reads become much cheaper, but random-access tail latency fails the screening guard.

blocks.takeaway: Sequential average -84.7%; random p99 +10.5%
blocks.x_label: Latency relative to original (100) — lower is better
blocks.note: Each dot is one paired run. Original latency = 100. The two rows measure different parts of the workload.

blocks.text: Decision: stop this candidate. Random p99 increased beyond its 3% allowance. The sequential benefit is promising, but needs a new design that protects the tail.

sections.title: 2. Decompress nearby pages ahead
sections.lead: Idea: put neighboring compressed pages into the swap cache before demand. This makes many reads cheap, while some faults pay for several pages at once.

blocks.takeaway: Average -0.4%: effectively unchanged; p99 +280.8%
blocks.x_label: Latency relative to original (100) — lower is better
blocks.note: Each dot is one paired run. Original latency = 100. The two rows measure different parts of the workload.

blocks.text: Decision: stop this candidate. Its average change is inside 3% noise; p99 exceeds the 7.73% allowance. Inference: synchronous decompression concentrates work into fewer, longer faults, rather than reducing total work.

sections.title: What we learned — and what to try next

blocks.takeaway: Keep the useful mechanism; address its cost
rows: Adapt the prefetch window to access behavior
Keep the sequential gain without a random-tail regression.
Bound the work performed on a demand fault
Reduce total latency without concentrating decompression into long stalls.

blocks.text: Evidence strength: two independent pairs per workload, after baseline noise calibration. Both candidates passed correctness checks but failed fast performance screening. No slow confirmation was run; new hypotheses require a new experiment.

blocks.text: Fast screening uses few pairs; failed guards block confirmation. Observed differences do not establish persistent causal effects. Unchanged-path outliers are not mechanism evidence.
